method: Source-of-record check at authoring time, then a separate second pass re-reading every numeric and quoted claim against the page it came from. Author and checker are the same pass, which is not the independent arrangement the older batches used.

findings.claim: The 35 C wet-bulb threshold came from Sherwood and Huber's 2010 theoretical study as an upper adaptability limit based on biophysical principles rather than empirical testing
Empirical thresholds for heat stress compensability were closer to 30.6 C in warm-humid conditions, with a linear decrease across hotter and drier environments
Measured skin temperatures were 36-38.5 C against a theoretical 35 C; sweating is physiologically controlled; clothing impedes evaporation; participants were unacclimatised
Under 1-3.5 C of warming, parts of every continent except Antarctica see rapid increases in the frequency and extent of noncompensable heat
Because the distribution of extreme wet-bulb temperatures falls off steeply, a modest reduction in the threshold moves a large area and population across it
findings.sourceChecked: inference from the extreme-value framing of the cited paper
findings.note: Our reasoning, stated as such; no magnitude is attached to it.

findings.claim: Skin temperatures of 36-38.5 C, physiological control of sweat rate, clothing resistance and lack of acclimatisation all lower the tolerance threshold
The measured compensability threshold is closer to 30.6 C in warm-humid conditions, decreasing linearly in hotter and drier environments
Six hours is a common exposure assumption rather than a physiological constant
Age, medication and chronic illness lower the threshold below the laboratory value
findings.sourceChecked: not quoted from a source read in this pass
findings.note: Stated without figures. The papers we read used healthy participants and note the acclimatisation caveat; the wider vulnerability distribution was not sourced here.

findings.claim: The NWS defines the heat index as how hot it feels when relative humidity is factored in with air temperature
The index assumes shady, light wind conditions; full sunshine can raise values by up to 15 F; strong winds with hot dry air can be extremely hazardous
96 F at 65% relative humidity gives a heat index of 121 F
Different countries use differently calibrated heat indices, so the same weather gives different values
findings.note: Stated as a general property of index construction, without naming indices or jurisdictions.

findings.claim: Wet-bulb temperature is the lowest temperature reachable by evaporating water into air at constant pressure
findings.sourceChecked: definitional; the tolerance paper uses the same definition
findings.note: A definition rather than a quoted claim.

findings.claim: US daytime urban temperatures about 1-7 F higher and nighttime about 2-5 F higher than outlying areas
Causes include reduced vegetation, material properties, urban geometry, anthropogenic heat from vehicles and air conditioning, and weather
Electricity demand for air conditioning rises 1-9% for each 2 F increase in temperature
An average of 702 heat deaths per year in the US, 2004-2018
Urban streams experienced temperature surges as much as 18 F higher than forested streams
Consecutive hot nights have a larger physiological effect than a single hot afternoon
findings.note: Offered as the reason the nighttime figure matters; stated without a study or a figure.

findings.claim: Cooling electricity demand rises 1-9% for each 2 F increase in temperature
Anthropogenic heat from air conditioning contributes to the urban heat island
Gas turbine output and thermal plant capacity fall with rising ambient and cooling-water temperature, and transmission line ratings fall in hot still air
findings.note: Stated qualitatively with no derating figures, because we did not read a source giving them.

findings.claim: IEA figures for space cooling's share of electricity demand and the number of air conditioners
findings.note: The page we fetched carries buildings-sector totals and no cooling-specific statistics. No IEA cooling figures are cited.

findings.claim: A 10 F excursion gives a 5% to 45% demand increase at the ends of the stated elasticity range
findings.note: Our arithmetic, shown in the text.

findings.claim: An average of 702 heat deaths per year in the US, 2004-2018
Certificate-based counts record the immediate cause, so heat-precipitated cardiovascular and respiratory deaths are coded to those causes
findings.note: A description of how certification works rather than a quoted finding; no ratio between methods is given.

findings.claim: Excess mortality analysis recovers the wider effect but depends on baseline modelling choices and cannot identify individual deaths
Tolerance varies with age, medication and acclimatisation
